elements.texte:
[cheerful] Since the start of module 8, you’ve been building the database for NutriBoost’s wellness workshops.

In the previous lesson, you organized the data into five tables, linked by foreign keys.

To understand these links, you have to find each foreign key and the table it refers to.

To see these relationships more easily, we’ll build a UML class diagram.

We start with the customers, coaches, workshops and cards.
elements.avant: Map out the tables and their relationships before building the database.
elements.apres: Each thing to manage is represented by a class.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Each thing to manage is represented by a class.

It has a name and contains attributes.

Attributes are the information that describes it, like a customer’s first name, last name and email.

At this stage, we describe the classes and their attributes.

Primary and foreign keys will be added when we move to tables.

Your turn!

This line is an association.

It reads in the direction of the triangle: a coach leads workshops.

Two more associations follow: a customer enrolls in workshops, and owns a membership card.

Your turn!
This line is an association.

Two more associations follow: a customer enrolls in workshops, and owns a membership card.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The multiplicity says how many items of one class can be linked to a single item of the other.

For example, how many workshops can one coach lead?

We write the answer on the side of the Workshop class.

Your turn!

Each workshop is led by a single coach: we put 1 on the Coach class side.

A coach can lead zero, one or several workshops: we put zero dot dot star on the Workshop class side.

For enrolls in: a customer takes zero, one or several workshops, so zero dot dot star on the Workshop class side.

Your turn!

The Morning yoga workshop has no one enrolled yet, the Recovery workshop has three.

So we write zero dot dot star on the Customer class side.

The enrollment date shows when a customer enrolled in a specific workshop.

We put the enrollment date in Enrollment, an association class.

It holds the information specific to the link between a customer and a workshop.

It’s linked by a dotted line to the association between Customer and Workshop.

Finally, a customer owns one membership card or none, and a card has only one customer.
elements.avant: Two more associations follow: a customer enrolls in workshops, and owns a membership card.
elements.apres: The diagram is now complete: it shows the information to keep and the relationships between the classes.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Each class becomes a table, and its attributes become columns.

Here, we add a primary key ID to identify each row uniquely.

The tables are defined.

Now the diagram’s relationships have to be turned into links between these tables.

First, we look at the maximum on each side.

1 means “at most one”, and star means “possibly many”.

These maximums tell three cases apart: one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many.

Each workshop has a single coach.

So we add coach underscore ID to the workshops table.

This foreign key shows which coach leads each workshop.

We add customer underscore ID to the cards table to show its owner.

The UNIQUE constraint prevents giving several cards to the same customer.

A customer can enroll in several workshops, and a workshop can welcome several customers.

Your turn!

So we create the enrollments table, with customer underscore ID, workshop underscore ID and enrollment underscore date.

It holds one row per enrollment.

The enrollments table links each customer to a workshop with the foreign keys customer underscore ID and workshop underscore ID.

It also keeps the enrollment date, from the association class.

You can apply these same rules to create the tables for the whole shop.

To do this, add the orders and the products to the diagram.

Your turn!

A customer places orders, and each order is for a single product.

In the next lesson, you’ll create these tables with CREATE TABLE.
